title: Gideon's fleece (Judges 6:36–40)
hookLine: Gideon asks twice for a sign, and receives it

lines: A FLEECE ON THE THRESHING FLOOR.
cards: Gideon lays a piece of wool, a fleece, on the threshing floor. Around him, everything is moving. The armies of Midian have crossed over and camped in the valley of Jezreel.
Gideon has blown the shofar, and men from several tribes are gathering behind him. He has already been told he'll save Israel. He has already seen fire leap from a rock to take his offering.
And still he wants one more sign, and he asks for it to come down with the dew.

teach.h: DEW ON THE FLEECE, THE GROUND DRY.
teach.b: If there's dew on the fleece only, he says, and the ground around it is dry, then I'll know you will save Israel by my hand, as you said. In the morning he gets up early and wrings out a bowl full of water.
The ground is dry. That should be enough. It isn't.

teach.h: LET NOT THINE ANGER BE HOT.
teach.b: So he asks again, and listen to how: "Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once."
This time, reverse it: a dry fleece, and dew on all the ground. And that night, the text says, God did so. Dry wool, wet earth.
What the story leaves out is any anger. No rebuke, no lecture on faith. The sign is given, and given again, without a word of complaint.
That matters, because the Torah also says not to put the Lord to the test. So readers argue over Gideon. Some say he was wrong to ask.
Some say he wasn't asking about God at all, but about himself: was he really the one? The story doesn't settle it.
It keeps the record: a frightened man doubted, said so out loud, politely, twice, and was answered both times.

how: Jews read the fleece story in Judges 6 as part of the Former Prophets, and commentators debate whether Gideon's request was a forbidden test of God or a plea for reassurance.

o: a doubter's sign, asked for twice and given twice
a war banner Gideon carried against Midian
a wool offering burned on the rock by the oak

games.q: doubt is allowed — tap the pairs.
p: dew on the fleece, dry ground
dry fleece, dew on the ground
a bowl full of water wrung out

s: God was angry at Gideon for asking twice
the text records no anger: the sign is simply given, both times.
the second time, Gideon asked for the fleece to stay dry
he reversed the test: a dry fleece and dew on all the ground.
the Torah says nothing about testing God
it says not to put the Lord to the test, which is why readers argue about the fleece.

games.q: you're Gideon. the fleece came up soaked and the ground dry, just as you asked. you're still not sure. what do you do?
o: ask once more, gently, with the test reversed.
games.why: he asks again, beginning 'let not thine anger be hot against me', and that night the fleece is dry and the ground is wet.

practice: Let one honest doubt come up, about a decision, about yourself, or about God if that's where it lives, and name it plainly, the way Gideon did, without arguing it away or scolding it.
Breathe with it beside you, as if it's allowed in the room. If you pray, bring it with his opening words: let not thine anger be hot against me.

wordCard.voice: Gideon's fleece. Wet when the ground was dry, then dry when the ground was wet: a doubter's sign, asked for twice and given twice.

orig.note: Hebrew: a fleece of wool, the one Gideon lays on the threshing floor in Judges 6:37.

carryVoice: Your line: doubt is allowed. Asking twice didn't make him less chosen. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once
